source.title: Test Accuracy vs. Generalization Gap: Model Selection in NLP without Accessing Training or Testing Data
source.authors: Yaoqing Yang; Ryan Theisen; Liam Hodgkinson; Joseph E. Gonzalez; K. Ramchandran; Charles H. Martin; Michael W. Mahoney

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to be the full technical report, including appendices; it is not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: Tests generalization-metric correlations in NLP Transformers, extending prior metric analyses to a different task and model family.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates many metrics against test BLEU and the training–test generalization gap. Its stated findings about shape and scale metrics are included below. Other metric-specific correlation values appear only in figures and are not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The record incorrectly says magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance was not tested. Appendix A.6 defines weight-scaled Gaussian perturbations constrained by training-loss increase and pacbayes_mag_flatness = 1/σ′². Figures 4, 10 and 16 evaluate this metric against the generalization gap in NLP Transformers, extending V7 to a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: popular metrics correlate well with the generalization gap in the evaluated NLP settings, while heavy-tail metrics appear more useful for predicting model quality without data access. The authors acknowledge weaknesses, including suboptimally trained models.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates correlations of weight-based, margin-based, and PAC-Bayesian metrics on WMT14 Transformers trained from scratch and pretrained Huggingface Transformers; it does not perform the magnitude-aware perturbation comparison described in V7.
record.method_sensitivity: Metric performance varies with training hyperparameters and model class; shape metrics can be anti-correlated for suboptimally trained models, and results for some metrics change with model width, dataset size, or normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Heavy-tail shape metrics often predict test BLEU better than scale metrics, while scale metrics better predict the training–test gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Predicting generalization-gap rankings need not predict held-out model-quality rankings in NLP Transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: Pretrained Transformer selection favors shape metrics overall, but correlations are modest and some metrics reverse their predictions across depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-spectrum metrics for pretrained NLP model selection depend on the metric and architecture comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 3 contrasts dropout 0.1 with no dropout and describes underfitting versus overfitting in translation Transformers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout changes training and held-out BLEU trajectories in translation Transformers.

record.problems: The study reports correlation analyses rather than causal evidence. Many metric-specific correlation results are presented only in figures, and metric values are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained: relevant metric-specific outcomes are shown in figures without readable reported values or a textual result attributable to the exact V7 measure. The paper's broader shape-versus-scale findings do not directly establish magnitude-aware sharpness as defined in V7.

untested.parts: Fitting random labels and comparing held-out performance with natural-label training.
Widening beyond a demonstrated zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Held-out error comparisons in fully connected or convolutional classifiers; the dropout illustration instead concerns translation Transformers.

The original convolutional-family, similarly low training-loss setting on CIFAR-10 and SVHN. This extension uses training-loss tolerance rather than training-error tolerance and a BLEU-based generalization gap.
Retraining after removing highly memorized versus random examples.

missing.what: Correct the assertion that the V7 measure was not evaluated and add magnitude-aware-flatness gap-correlation rows, preserving separate epoch-wise, learning-rate, width and sample-size conditions. Figure-only outcomes were declared omitted, but their relevance to V7 was incorrectly rejected. Ordered rankings are readable; correlation magnitudes and signs cannot reliably be recovered from the supplied text.
missing.locator: Appendix A.6, equations 24 and 30; Figures 4b, 10a–d and 16b

record.verdict_notes: There are no existing rows to fix. Comparative rankings support the conditional verdicts above, but do not establish correlation magnitudes, statistical significance, or an absent or reversed sharpness–gap relationship.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and generalization on natural labels.
Width beyond interpolation and test error.

The study compares generalization metrics, including PAC-Bayesian magnitude-aware metrics, but does not directly test magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance as the version defines it. Metric-specific results are figure-only.

relationships.condition: WMT14 Transformers, varying learning rate with other hyperparameters fixed; comparative ranking component.
relationships.reason: Figure 10a ranks magnitude-aware flatness first by median gap correlation, ahead of the tested norm and margin metrics. Based on the figure's ordered metric names; no extracted row or readable correlation magnitude is available.
relationships.display_finding: The available evidence does not confirm that sharpness ranked BLEU gaps better than norm and margin measures.
